segments: 1. Flake = specification; lock = resolved instance
flake.nix describes the dependencies (dependency specification), while flake.lock pins their resolved instances (dependency resolution).
Without flake.lock, nixos-unstable always points to the latest commit, making builds unreproducible. Reproducibility comes from (flake.nix + flake.lock).
2. Why the update covers all of nixpkgs
Nix manages a package set, rather than an individual package.

Updating the nixpkgs input replaces the definition of the entire package set, potentially changing multiple applications and shared dependencies together. Actual builds involve only the closure required by the configuration.

To track a newer version of just one application, you can introduce a second nixpkgs input and select that package from it, or maintain an overlay, a separate Flake package, or a derivation with pinned source code. These approaches can still introduce different dependencies, so check compatibility. They are not equivalent to an in-place, single-package upgrade with a traditional package manager.

5. Generations and the Store
A generation is not a copy of the system, but a set of symbolic links into /nix/store.
Therefore:
Generations are lightweight.
When the closure is complete, the corresponding build outputs can be reused; evaluation still needs the referenced sources and other inputs.
Downloads or builds are needed only for items missing from the Store.

10. Key takeaways

Updating the nixpkgs input changes the package set; Nix can also manage derivations and packages independently. The minimum unit of reproducibility is not the configuration alone, but (flake.nix + flake.lock). System state is not a collection of files, but the reference relationship Generation → Store.
Most seemingly "inconvenient" design choices, such as dependency-graph updates, strict hash verification, and pinned inputs, serve the same goal: reproducibility and consistency.
